questions.why: Ojukwu fled to Ivory Coast; Effiong surrendered in Lagos. Orizu was the acting Senate President who handed power to Ironsi in 1966, and Akintola was killed in the January coup.

questions.q: Which power supplied the Federal Military Government with aircraft and advisers?
options: France
Portugal
The USSR
The United Kingdom
questions.concept: Who backed which side in the civil war
questions.why: The USSR backed the federal side with aircraft and advisers. France and Portugal supplied Biafra; the UK, like the US, chose neutrality.

checks.topic: Basic JavaScript: declaration keywords, comparison operators, array methods, loops and ways to define a function.

questions.q: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
options: let
const
var
function
questions.concept: const is the read-only declaration keyword
questions.why: const is read-only, so reassigning it throws a TypeError. let and var can both be reassigned; function defines a function, not a variable.

questions.q: What does the strict equal operator check that the equal operator does not?
options: That both values are truthy
That neither value is undefined
That both operands are variables
That the two values are of the same data type
questions.concept: === compares value and data type; == compares value only
questions.why: 5 == "5" is true but 5 === "5" is false, because === also requires the data types to match. Truthiness, undefined checks and being a variable have nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Which array method returns a new array of the elements passing a test?
options: filter()
forEach()
splice()
push()
questions.concept: filter() returns a new array; forEach() returns nothing
questions.why: filter() builds and returns a new array of the elements that pass. forEach() only runs a function once per element, splice() adds or removes at an index, and push() adds to the end.

questions.q: Which loop always runs its block at least once?
options: for
while
do-while
for with a false condition
questions.concept: do-while checks its condition after the block runs
questions.why: In do-while the condition is checked after the body, so the body always runs once. for and while both test first and may run zero times.

questions.q: Which form of function is defined and executed immediately, creating a private scope?
options: An arrow function
An IIFE
A function declaration
An object constructor
questions.concept: The IIFE and its private scope
questions.why: An IIFE is wrapped in parentheses and invoked on the spot, so its variables stay hidden outside. Arrow functions are a concise ES6 form, declarations are named and called later, and constructors build object instances with new.

checks.topic: The three stages of the writing process, and naming pre-writing techniques and post-writing activities.

questions.q: What are the three stages of the writing process, in order?
options: Pre-writing, during-writing, post-writing
Drafting, pre-writing, publishing
Planning, proofreading, revising
Pre-writing, post-writing, during-writing
questions.concept: The ordered three stages of the writing process
questions.why: The lecture names pre-writing, then during-writing or drafting, then post-writing. Option 4 has the last two reversed; the others mix single activities in as if they were stages.

questions.q: Which post-writing activity is limited to typos, misspellings and punctuation?
options: Revision
Editing for grammar and style
Peer review
Proofreading
questions.concept: Proofreading is surface-level only
questions.why: Proofreading catches surface slips and comes last. Revision changes content and paragraph order, editing works at sentence and word level, and peer review is feedback from another writer.

questions.q: A poet associates words and images around a central theme. Which technique is that?
options: Listing
Outlining
Clustering
Storyboarding
questions.concept: Clustering as association around a core idea
questions.why: Clustering radiates creative associations from one central theme, and the poet is the deck's own example. Listing is a linear enumeration, outlining fixes sequence and hierarchy, and storyboarding plans scenes visually.

questions.q: Which post-writing step marks the end of the writing process?
options: Finalising conclusions
Publishing or submitting
Formatting and presentation
Checking citations and references
questions.concept: Publishing or submitting ends the process
questions.why: Publishing or submitting hands the work to its intended audience and ends the process. The other three are earlier post-writing activities, not the closing step.

questions.q: Which pre-writing technique produces a roadmap of key points and logical flow?
options: Free-writing
Brainstorming
Research
Outlining
questions.concept: Outlining produces the roadmap
questions.why: Outlining sets out key points, supporting evidence and a logical flow, giving structure and direction. Free-writing is continuous unstructured prose, brainstorming yields an unfiltered pool of ideas, and research gathers facts and evidence.

checks.topic: Verifying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: its basis, the circuit equations, the sign rules, the procedure and a negative current.

questions.q: Which conservation principle is Kirchhoff's Voltage Law based on?
options: Conservation of charge
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of energy
Conservation of current
questions.concept: KVL rests on conservation of energy
questions.why: KVL says the algebraic sum of voltage drops around a closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy around a path. Conservation of charge is what KCL, the node rule, expresses.

questions.q: Which of these is the KCL node equation in this experiment?
options: I3R3 + I3R4 + I1R5 = E1
E1 + E2 = I3R3
questions.concept: Telling a node equation from a loop equation
questions.why: A KCL equation is written at a node and contains currents only. The other three all contain IR products or emfs, so they have units of volts and are loop equations.

questions.q: By the deck's rule, when is an emf counted as positive?
options: When the battery drives current in the assumed direction
When the battery is traversed from its positive to its negative terminal
When the battery is traversed from its negative to its positive terminal
When the loop is traversed clockwise
questions.concept: The deck's battery sign rule
questions.why: The deck counts an emf positive when the source is traversed from positive terminal to negative terminal. Option 3 is the opposite convention, and the sign does not depend on the current direction or on which way round the page you walk.

questions.q: The solution gives I2 as negative. What does that mean?
options: A resistance value was substituted wrongly
The ammeter was connected with reversed polarity
The current in that branch is decreasing with time
The real current runs opposite to the direction assumed on the diagram
questions.concept: A negative current means a reversed assumption, not an error
questions.why: The magnitude is still correct; only the assumed arrow was drawn the wrong way. It is not an arithmetic mistake, and the currents here are steady, not changing with time.

questions.q: After the first recording, in what interval is the emf stepped up?
options: 1 V
3 V
9 V
questions.concept: The 3 V step in the procedure
questions.why: The emf is increased at regular 3 V intervals, so the sample runs at 9, 12 and 15 V. 9 V is the starting emf and 50 V is the maximum output range set before dialling.

recapCandidates.topic: The arrows you draw for the branch currents are not a guess you have to get right; they are a definition of which direction counts as positive in each branch. The signs in a loop equation are then fixed by the direction you walk the loop, not by the direction the current really flows. A current that comes out negative is a correct answer with the arrow drawn the other way round.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students believe the arrows are a prediction that must be correct before the equations are valid, so a negative current reads to them as an error to be hunted down; the belief survives because in every single-loop circuit with one battery the obvious guess really is the true direction, so guessing right and being right never come apart until a second emf is introduced.
whyQuestions: Why are we allowed to draw a current arrow before we know which way the current actually flows?
Why does the sign of an IR term depend on the direction you walk the loop, while the sign of an emf term does not?
Why does reversing one arrow change nothing except the sign of that one current in the answer?
Why does a negative current in the answer not mean an equation was written wrongly, and what test separates the two cases?
Why can you draw all three branch arrows pointing into the same node and still get the right answer out?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says the arrow defines what counts as positive current in that branch, and that every junction and loop equation is then written consistently with that definition, so the physics enters only through the emfs, the resistances and the way the circuit is wired.
It says both Kirchhoff rules are linear in the currents, so replacing a current by its negative reproduces the same system; a reversed definition therefore returns the same magnitude with the opposite sign, and the answer is read off, not redone.
It gives the discriminating test between a reversed arrow and a real mistake: put the solution back into the junction equation and every loop equation, and check the power balance; if they all close, the minus sign is physical and means the current runs against the arrow.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Nodes a (top) and b (bottom) are joined by three parallel branches: a 12 V battery with internal resistance 1 ohm, a 6 V battery with internal resistance 1 ohm (both positive terminals towards a), and a 4 ohm resistor. Assume I1 and I2 flow b to a inside the batteries and I3 flows a to b through the resistor. Junction rule at a: I3 = I1 + I2. Loop with the 12 V battery and the resistor, walked b to a then a to b: enter the battery at minus and leave at plus for +12, traverse r1 with the current for -(1)I1, traverse the 4 ohm with I3 for -4I3, giving 12 - I1 - 4I3 = 0. The same walk on the second branch gives 6 - I2 - 4I3 = 0. Hence I1 = 12 - 4I3 and I2 = 6 - 4I3; substituting into the junction equation, I3 = 18 - 8I3, so 9I3 = 18 and I3 = 2.0 A. Then I1 = 4.0 A and I2 = 6 - 8 = -2.0 A. The minus sign is the whole point: the 6 V branch really carries 2.0 A from a to b, into its own positive terminal, so that battery is being charged. Check the answer three ways: the junction gives 4.0 + (-2.0) = 2.0 A; V_ab is 12 - 4.0(1) = 8.0 V along branch one, 6 - (-2.0)(1) = 8.0 V along branch two and 2.0 x 4 = 8.0 V along the resistor; and the power balance gives 12 x 4.0 = 48 W delivered against 16 + 4 + 16 = 36 W dissipated plus 6 x 2.0 = 12 W absorbed by the charging battery, which is 48 W.

recapCandidates.topic: On a flowchart, a loop is not a symbol - it is a decision diamond plus a flow line that runs backwards. Which boxes get repeated is decided entirely by where that backward arrow lands, so moving the arrow by one box changes the algorithm even though every box still says exactly what it said before.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students read a flowchart the way they read a page, top to bottom, and treat the boxes as the meaning and the arrows as joining-up; this works perfectly for pure sequence and for selection, where the arrows do run downward, so it survives every chart until the first one with a back arrow.
whyQuestions: Why does the diamond need two exits when a rectangle needs only one?
Why can the same diamond mean selection in one chart and repetition in another - what in the drawing tells them apart?
Why does a loop whose counter is incremented on the exit branch run forever, when the increment box is plainly there on the page?
Why does moving the back arrow from below Sum = 0 to above it change what the chart prints, when not one box has been edited?
Why can you not tell how many times a loop runs by reading its condition, and what must you do instead?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Names the mechanism: the flow lines, not the vertical layout, define the repeated circuit - every symbol between the back arrow's landing point and the diamond runs again on each pass, everything above it runs once.
Shows the consequence in both directions: initialisation caught inside the circuit is undone every pass (the accumulator loses its total, or the counter resets and the loop never ends), and an update stranded outside the circuit never executes, so the diamond re-evaluates identical data and answers identically forever.
Gives the test to apply to any chart: find the backward arrow, mark the symbols it encloses, then trace a table of variable values pass by pass rather than reading the condition and trusting what it sounds like.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Draw the lecture's chart at the board: Start; Count = 0; Sum = 0; then label the next box A: Enter n; Sum = Sum + n; Count = Count + 1; then the diamond 'Is Count < 5?' with Yes running back to A and No running to Print Sum; Stop. Trace it with 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 in a three-column table (n, Sum, Count): pass 1 gives 2, 2, 1; pass 2 gives 4, 6, 2; pass 3 gives 6, 12, 3; pass 4 gives 8, 20, 4; pass 5 gives 10, 30, 5, at which point 5 < 5 is false and 30 is printed. Now change nothing except the back arrow, so that it lands on Sum = 0 instead of on A, and re-trace: Count is still outside the loop and still climbs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the chart still exits after five passes, but Sum is cleared at the top of every pass, giving 2, then 4, then 6, then 8, then 10, and the chart prints 10. Finally move the arrow up one box further, onto Count = 0: now the counter resets too, the diamond is handed Count = 1 on every pass, 1 < 5 is true forever and the chart never reaches Print Sum. Three algorithms, identical boxes, one arrow moved twice.
